newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Gunmen bar premier's route in lawless Albania.
newsitem.headline: Gunmen bar premier's route in lawless Albania.

text.p: Heavily-armed men barred Albanian premier Bashkim Fino from visiting a town north of Tirana on Saturday in a new spasm of lawlessness as Albania waited impatiently for the arrival of an Italian-led security force.

About 15 gunmen blocked Fino and other cabinet ministers at Bushat, 100 km (60 miles) north of Tirana, as the officials drove in convoy to the town of Shkoder. The gunmen detonated two grenades on the roadside and forced him to turn back to Tirana.
"This was a grave incident," Fino said after meeting ministers back in Tirana. "The national reconciliation government has openly said it will travel everywhere in Albania."

Finance Minister Arben Malaj, who travelled with Fino, said the gunmen claimed 120 people from Shkoder were being held in the southern port of Sarande and demanded their release. Malaj denied the claims but said the government would check.
Separately, President Sali Berisha was quoted as criticising Europe's slowness in sending a 6,000-strong force to help protect aid to the ex-communist state after an insurrection last month.

"The president called for an urgent procedure because he said 'we need the assistance of Europe and it takes too long up to now'," said Rene van der Linden, the Dutch head of a Council of Europe delegation who met Berisha on Saturday.
He said Berisha had no doubt that the force would be deployed. Italy said on Friday it would not be ready until April 14 at the earliest.

Much of southern Albania is controlled by rebel councils demanding Berisha's resignation after protests over the collapse of savings schemes spilled over into a nationwide uprising last month. Weapons depots have been looted and banditry is rife.

Saturday's challenge to Fino showed that even the north is not fully under government control. Fino is a Socialist from southern Albania and a long-time opponent of right-winger Berisha, who draws the strongest support from the north.

The Albanian news agency ATA said the government representative in Shkoder, on hearing of the incident, reaffirmed the region's support for the all-party crisis government appointed by Berisha on March 11.
Earlier, ATA said Fino spoke to Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini to stress that Albanians wanted the international force, due to protect deliveries of food and medicines.

"The Italian troops will have maximum security and complete support from the Albanian government and public opinion," Fino told Dini on Friday night. Italy's parliament is to vote next week on deployment.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Saturday dismissed talk that his government could fall in a rift with a key ally over his plan to send Italian troops to Albania.

"The government I lead was not born for a short life," he said. Prodi is facing the toughest political challenge of his 11 months in office over the refusal of the hard-left Communist Refoundation party to back the deployment of the first Italian-led multinational force in post-World War Two history.
In Tirana, Italian politician Pierferdinando Casini, of the opposition Christian Democratic Centre party, met Berisha and affirmed that his party would vote for deployment.
He said he agreed with Berisha that unrest was triggered by mafia-like groups and ex-communist secret police.

Debate about deployment has been overshadowed by the sinking of a packed Albanian refugee vessel off Italy on March 28 in a collision with an Italian navy corvette. Tirana says at least 80 people died and many of the 34 survivors accused Italy of ramming the boat, something Italy denies.
Italy is expected to provide between 2,000 and 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Romania 400 and Spain 300. Austria and Denmark say they are also considering participation.
